title: The hard passages
hook: some passages are troubling; teachers and communities read them honestly, in context

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rule in tractate Gittin: feed the poor and visit the sick of every people, and your line, for the ways of peace. Who outside your circle did you help? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-two.

A sentence lifted off a page of Talmud can travel a long way. Sometimes it turns up online, cut loose from everything around it, offered as proof that the whole book is cruel. Sometimes a student meets one in class and goes quiet. Either way, the question underneath is real. The Talmud is a huge record of argument, and some of what its sages said is hard to read today: lines about women, about outsiders, about punishment. Careful teachers don't pretend those lines aren't there. What they do with them is today's lesson.
screen: `A SENTENCE CUT LOOSE.` → `SOME LINES ARE HARD TO READ.` → `WHAT TEACHERS DO WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Read in context. It sounds simple. It's a discipline. Start with who is speaking. A page of Talmud is a conversation, so a line may be one sage's view, raised so the next sage can push against it. A view on the page isn't automatically a ruling. Then ask what the page is arguing about, and what came just before. Then ask what later law did with it: some statements were set aside, and some were read so narrowly they almost never applied. The Talmud itself shows this move with one of the hardest laws in the Torah. Deuteronomy describes a stubborn and rebellious son, brought by his parents to the elders of the city. The sages read that passage so closely, word by word, condition by condition, that a teaching in tractate Sanhedrin says such a son never was and never will be. Then why was it written? The answer given: study it, and receive reward. A hard verse becomes a reason to study, not a sentence to carry out. But context isn't an eraser. Some passages stay hard after all the explaining, and teachers who take the text seriously say so out loud. Communities respond in different ways. Some read a hard line as belonging to its own time and place. Some search the commentators for the reading that guards a person's dignity. Some name the hurt plainly and keep studying beside it. What they share is a refusal of two shortcuts: hiding the passage, or waving it around without its page. Read the whole page first. Then judge it.
screen: `WHO IS SPEAKING?` · `WHAT IS THE PAGE ARGUING?` · `A SON WHO NEVER WAS.` · `CONTEXT IS NOT AN ERASER.` · then, large: `READ THE WHOLE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to read one hard text slowly. Choose a line from any book that troubles you, scripture or not, or recall one you already know. Settle, and let your breath slow. Hold the line in mind. Ask who is speaking. Ask what came just before it. Ask whom it might hurt, and whom it might have been meant to protect in its own day. Don't rush to fix it or to throw it out. Let it stay hard for a moment, and keep breathing beside it. When your mind runs ahead to a verdict, come back to the words themselves. The bell holds the time.
The hard passages. Lines in the Talmud that trouble readers today, which Jewish teachers read honestly, in context, without hiding them and without cutting them loose. Today's word.

Your line: read in context. Today, when a quotation reaches you without its page, from any source, look up what came before and after it before you decide what it means. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Jewish teachers and study partners often stop at a troubling passage to ask who is speaking, what the discussion is about, and how later commentators and codes treated it. Communities differ in how they explain and respond to such passages.

Sanhedrin 71a ('there never was a stubborn and rebellious son and there never will be; why was it written? study and receive reward') is paraphrased. The Talmud also records a dissenting view (Rabbi Yonatan says he saw one); the script says 'a teaching' rather than 'the Talmud says' for that reason. Please confirm the framing.

The script deliberately does not quote any specific troubling passage about women or non-Jews; it names those topics generally. Please confirm the description of how communities respond is fair and complete enough.
